title: Secure Coding Practices
description: Preventing injection, XSS, broken access control, and auth flaws in application code (OWASP Top 10).

questions.prompt: This lookup function uses psycopg (PostgreSQL). Which change prevents SQL injection?

options.text: Reject any username containing the words SELECT, DROP, or UNION
`cur.execute("SELECT id, email FROM users WHERE username = %s", (username,))`
Check that the username is shorter than 32 characters before querying
Run the query inside a transaction so injected statements can be rolled back

questions.explanation: A parameterized query sends the value separately from the SQL text, so input can never change the query's structure (OWASP A03:2021 Injection). Keyword blocklists are easily bypassed, for example by `' OR '1'='1`, which contains none of those words.

questions.prompt: This page greets the visitor using a name from the URL. Which change fixes the cross-site scripting vulnerability while still displaying the name?

options.text: Assign the greeting to `textContent` instead of `innerHTML`
Remove `<script>` tags from `name` with a regex before inserting it
Read the name from a POST body instead of the query string
Serve the page only over HTTPS with a valid certificate

questions.prompt: A sign-up service must store user passwords so they can be verified at login. Which approach is appropriate?

options.text: Encrypt with AES-256 and keep the key in an environment variable
Hash with SHA-256 using a unique per-user salt for each password
Hash with Argon2id (or bcrypt) using a unique salt and a tuned work factor
Store them as plaintext in a column only the auth service can read

questions.explanation: Passwords should be one-way hashed with a deliberately slow, salted algorithm such as Argon2id, scrypt, or bcrypt (OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet; ASVS V2.4). Salted SHA-256 is fast, so GPUs can test billions of guesses per second, and encryption is reversible by anyone who gets the key.

questions.prompt: True or false: because the sign-up form's JavaScript rejects usernames containing `<` or `'`, the server-side handler does not need to validate the username.
questions.explanation: Attackers can bypass the browser entirely and send requests with curl or an intercepting proxy, so client-side checks are only a usability feature. Validation must be enforced on the server (ASVS V5).

questions.prompt: When it fails, a production login endpoint returns the response below to users. What is the appropriate fix from a security standpoint?

code.source:
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: text/plain

psycopg2.errors.UndefinedColumn: column "pasword_hash" does not exist
  File "/srv/app/auth/login.py", line 31, in login
    cur.execute("SELECT id, pasword_hash FROM users WHERE email = %s", ...)

options.text: Stop logging the error at all so the details are never recorded anywhere
Return HTTP 200 with the same body so scanners don't flag a 500 status
Base64-encode the stack trace before sending it so it is not human-readable
Return a generic error with a reference ID and log the full details server-side

questions.explanation: Stack traces reveal file paths, queries, and schema details that help attackers (OWASP A05:2021 Security Misconfiguration). Users should get a generic message and a correlation ID, while engineers get full details in server logs. Base64 is an encoding, not protection.

questions.prompt: This Express route should let a logged-in user fetch only their own invoices. `requireLogin` verifies the session and sets `req.user`. Which line contains the access-control flaw?
questions.explanation: Line 6 compares the owner to a user ID supplied by the client in the query string, so an attacker just passes the victim's ID (an IDOR, OWASP A01:2021 Broken Access Control). It must compare against the server-side identity, `req.user.id`. Returning 404 rather than 403 on line 7 is deliberate, to avoid confirming that the invoice exists.

questions.prompt: After login on https://app.example.com, the server sets the session cookie shown below. Which attributes should be added to harden it? Select all that apply.

options.text: Domain=.example.com
HttpOnly
Secure
SameSite=Lax

questions.explanation: HttpOnly blocks JavaScript from reading the cookie, Secure keeps it off plain HTTP, and SameSite=Lax stops it from being sent on most cross-site requests (CSRF). Adding a Domain widens it to every subdomain, and a one-year Max-Age extends the window for session theft (ASVS V3.4).

questions.prompt: What is the most serious risk in this Flask route, and the right fix?

options.text: A crafted cookie can run arbitrary code when unpickled; use validated JSON or keep prefs server-side
Base64 isn't encryption, so users can read their own prefs; encrypt the cookie with AES
Pickled data can exceed the 4 KB cookie limit; compress it before Base64-encoding it
pickle is slow for every request; switch to the marshal module for faster loading

questions.explanation: Unpickling attacker-controlled data executes code chosen by the attacker (OWASP A08:2021 Software and Data Integrity Failures), and Python's docs warn never to unpickle untrusted data. Users reading their own preferences is harmless; the danger is the deserializer itself.

questions.prompt: What is wrong with this Express middleware, which uses the jsonwebtoken library?

options.text: The token should come from a cookie, because Authorization headers can't carry JWTs
Returning 403 reveals that the route exists; the middleware should return 404 instead
`jwt.decode()` doesn't check the signature, so anyone can forge an admin token; use `jwt.verify()`
Optional chaining lets requests without an Authorization header skip the role check

questions.explanation: jsonwebtoken's `decode()` only parses the payload; `verify()` checks the signature (and expiry) against your key, and should be given an explicit `algorithms` list. With no header, `token` is undefined, `decode` returns null, and the request still gets 403.

questions.prompt: A link-preview feature fetches any URL a user submits and returns the page title. It runs on a cloud VM. A tester submits `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` and gets data back. Which mitigation is most effective?

options.text: Reject any URL whose text contains "169.254.169.254" or "localhost"
Resolve the host, block private/loopback/link-local IPs on every redirect, and enforce IMDSv2
Accept only URLs that begin with https:// so plain-HTTP targets are refused
Strip the path so the server fetches only the root page of the given host

questions.explanation: SSRF defenses (OWASP A10:2021) must check the IP address actually connected to, including after redirects, because string blocklists miss decimal IPs, DNS names that resolve internally, and redirects. IMDSv2's session-token requirement adds defense in depth for the metadata service. An https:// URL can still redirect to an internal address.

questions.prompt: Users should be able to change only their `displayName` and `bio`. The User model also has `role` and `emailVerified` fields. What is the fix for this Sequelize route?

options.text: Remove `role` and `emailVerified` from the JSON returned by the user API
Add CSRF protection to the route so only the real user can submit changes
Check that req.body is well-formed JSON before passing it to `update()`
Update only allowlisted fields, e.g., `user.update({ displayName, bio })` taken from req.body

questions.explanation: Passing the whole request body lets a user send `{"role": "admin"}` (mass assignment, OWASP API3:2023 Broken Object Property Level Authorization). Allowlisting writable fields closes it, while hiding fields from responses or adding CSRF protection doesn't stop a logged-in user from setting them.

questions.prompt: This helper must serve files only from inside /srv/app/uploads. Other directories with sensitive data exist alongside it under /srv/app/. Which line lets a crafted filename escape the intended directory?
questions.explanation: A string-prefix check accepts sibling directories: `../uploads_private/report.csv` resolves to /srv/app/uploads_private/report.csv, which starts with /srv/app/uploads. Compare whole path components instead, e.g., `os.path.commonpath([UPLOAD_ROOT, path]) == UPLOAD_ROOT`. The `realpath` call on line 8 correctly resolves `..` and symlinks first.

questions.prompt: This function verifies a webhook's HMAC-SHA256 signature, sent as a hex string, on a public endpoint. Which line introduces a vulnerability?

code.source:
import hashlib
import hmac


def verify_webhook(secret: bytes, body: bytes, signature_hex: str) -> bool:
    expected = hmac.new(secret, body, hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
    return expected == signature_hex

questions.explanation: `==` can return as soon as it finds a difference, so response timing can leak how much of a forged signature is correct. Python's docs say to use `hmac.compare_digest()`, which runs in constant time. Computing the HMAC with SHA-256 on line 6 is correct.

questions.prompt: What is the most serious flaw in this password-reset token generator?

code.source:
def create_reset_token(user):
    raw = f"{user.email}:{int(time.time())}"
    token = hashlib.sha256(raw.encode()).hexdigest()
    db.save_reset(user.id, token, expires_in=timedelta(hours=24))
    send_email(user.email, f"https://app.example.com/reset?token={token}")

options.text: Anyone who knows the email and rough request time can compute the token; use `secrets.token_urlsafe(32)`
SHA-256 is unsuitable for tokens; switching to SHA-512 makes the generated token unguessable
The 24-hour lifetime is the core flaw; shortening it to 15 minutes makes this design safe
Tokens in URLs are inherently unsafe; the token should be sent as an email attachment instead

questions.explanation: The input is predictable (a known email plus a Unix timestamp that can be brute-forced across a few thousand seconds), so hashing it adds no secrecy, whatever the hash. Tokens need a CSPRNG with at least 128 bits of entropy, along with single use and short expiry (OWASP Forgot Password Cheat Sheet).

questions.prompt: A product list lets users choose the sort with `?sort=name`, `price`, or `created_at`. The query is otherwise parameterized. How should the sort column be added to the SQL safely?

options.text: Insert it with an f-string after escaping any single quotes in the value
Bind it as a query parameter: `ORDER BY %s` with `(sort,)`
Map the value through an allowlist of known column names and reject anything else
Strip spaces and semicolons from the value, then concatenate it into the query

questions.explanation: Placeholders bind values, not identifiers, so `ORDER BY %s` sorts by a string literal rather than a column (or errors). Identifiers must come from a server-side allowlist (OWASP SQL Injection Prevention Cheat Sheet). Quote-escaping or character stripping still lets attackers inject expressions such as `CASE WHEN ... END`.
